paragraphs.context: Well, we’ve been thinking about it for some time
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marilla explains why she and Matthew decided to adopt a child, and why they wanted a boy.
paragraphs.simple: Marilla says they have talked about it all winter. Mrs. Spencer will bring a girl from the orphan home in spring, so Marilla and Matthew thought of taking a boy. Matthew is sixty and not as quick as before, and his heart is not strong. It is hard to find help on a farm, because boys leave to work in the factories or in the United States. Marilla did not want a street child from London. She wanted a child born in Canada, and she believes she would feel better and sleep better.

paragraphs.context: Why, a bride, of course
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne talks about her wish for a white dress and the ugly dress she wore from the orphan home.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she imagines a bride in white. She thinks she is too plain to be a bride, perhaps only a missionary would marry her. Her greatest wish is a white dress. She has never had a pretty one, and she felt ashamed of the ugly cloth dress that all the orphans wore. People thought they pitied her on the train, so she imagined she had a beautiful dress.

paragraphs.context: When Marilla had gone Anne looked around her wistfully
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne sees her cold, bare room and cries herself to sleep.
paragraphs.simple: After Marilla left, Anne looked sadly around the room. The walls were white and bare, and the floor had only a round mat. There was an old bed, a small table with a hard red pincushion, a small mirror, a window with a white frill and a wash-stand. The room was stiff and cold. Anne cried, took off her clothes, put on a thin nightgown and hid under the bed covers. Marilla saw only the clothes on the floor and the untidy bed.

paragraphs.context: Oh, I don’t mean just the tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells Marilla how much she loves the morning, the brook and Green Gables.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she loves the whole world on a fine morning, not only the cherry tree. She loves the brook that laughs even under the ice, and she wants to remember that there is a brook at Green Gables even if she must leave. She is not in despair in the morning, but she is sad because it was only imagining that she could stay.

paragraphs.context: Well, I don’t know.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about her parents and her early life.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she read that a rose smells sweet with any name, but she does not believe it. Her mother was a teacher who stopped teaching when she married. They were poor and lived in a tiny yellow house, which Anne has only imagined, with honeysuckle and lilacs. She was born there. Mrs. Thomas said she was the plainest, thinnest baby, but her mother thought her beautiful.

paragraphs.context: And if there isn’t Mrs. Peter coming up the lane
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Spencer rushes into the cold parlour and talks fast because a lady has arrived.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Spencer is happy that Mrs. Peter is coming, because they can decide about Anne at once. She leads the guests to the cold parlour where the air feels dead. She tells Marilla to take the chair and tells Anne to sit still on the ottoman. She tells her helper to put the kettle on, introduces the ladies, and leaves to remove buns from the oven.

paragraphs.context: Well, I’ll do my best
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne prays in her own way and asks to stay at Green Gables and to be pretty.
paragraphs.simple: Anne promises to try and kneels, speaking in the style of the church. She thanks God for the places she has named and says she is grateful. She says there are too many things she wants, so she will mention two: to stay at Green Gables and to be good-looking when she grows up.

paragraphs.context: Oh, I’m so glad she’s pretty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about her imaginary friend Katie Maurice in the glass door of a bookcase.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says that, after being beautiful herself, the next best thing is a beautiful close friend. At Mrs. Thomas's house, she pretended her reflection in the glass door was a girl called Katie Maurice. She told Katie everything. They pretended the bookcase was magic and if Anne knew the spell she could go into Katie's world full of flowers and fairies.

paragraphs.context: Well, I see that I’ll have to be very careful what I say
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Rachel is offended and says Marilla should punish the child.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Rachel says in an angry, sarcastic way that she must now be careful what she says, because the feelings of an orphan must come first. She says she is not annoyed, only sorry for Marilla. She says Marilla should use a birch switch on the child and that the girl's temper matches her hair. She will not visit again soon if she may be insulted.

paragraphs.context: Oh, Mrs. Lynde, I am so extremely sorry
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne makes an over-dramatic apology.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she is so sorry that she cannot say it in all the words of a dictionary. She says she behaved terribly and disgraced Matthew and Marilla. She calls herself wicked and ungrateful and says she should be punished. She admits that what Mrs. Lynde said was true, but says she should not have lost her temper. She begs to be forgiven so that she will not suffer all her life.

paragraphs.context: Anne started off irreproachable
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne goes to Sunday school in a plain dress and decorates her hat with wild flowers.
paragraphs.simple: Anne set out looking perfect in a stiff black-and-white dress. It was long enough and not too small, but it made her thin body look angular. Her hat was plain, and she wanted ribbon and flowers. On the way she saw bright buttercups and wild roses and quickly made a wreath for her hat. She was happy with it and walked proudly.

paragraphs.context: “Oh yes,” sighed Anne, blissfully unconscious
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells happy news about her friendship with Diana.
paragraphs.simple: Anne is very happy and says she is the happiest girl on the island. She tells Marilla that she and Diana will build a playhouse and she wants broken china to use. Diana's birthday is in February and hers is in March, which she finds very strange. Diana will lend a book, show a place with lilies, teach a song and give her a picture. Anne wishes she had something to give Diana.

paragraphs.context: “I do not like patchwork,” said Anne dolefully
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne complains about sewing patchwork and talks about her playhouse.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she does not like patchwork because it needs no imagination and seems never to end. She still prefers to be Anne of Green Gables sewing than to be anywhere else with nothing to do. She tells about the little ring of birch trees across the brook where she and Diana have a playhouse called Idlewild, a name that took her a whole night to invent.

paragraphs.context: “I took the amethyst brooch,” said Anne
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne makes up a false confession about the brooch, with a long dramatic story.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says, like a learned lesson, that she took the amethyst brooch. She says she could not resist, because she wanted to play a lady in Idlewild. She walked the long way to have more time. On the bridge she took it off to look again and it slipped from her fingers into the lake. She tells this in a long, dramatic way.

paragraphs.context: “Indeed I was,” said Anne comfortably
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about her first day at school.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says school was not hard. She sits with Diana by the window and plays happily with the girls. She is behind the others in books but has a better imagination. The teacher said her spelling was disgraceful and showed her slate, and she felt ashamed. Other girls were kind and gave her gifts.

paragraphs.context: “I should think Marilla’s raspberry cordial
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells Diana about the cake she ruined while imagining a sad story.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says Marilla is a famous cook and is teaching her, but cooking gives little room for imagination. She tells how she forgot the flour in a cake because she was thinking of a sad story in which Diana is ill and Anne dies nursing her. She cried, the cake failed, and Marilla was cross.

paragraphs.context: Marilla pessimistically expected more trouble
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne and Gilbert become rivals at school, and Anne holds a grudge.
paragraphs.simple: Marilla expected more trouble when Anne went back to school, but none came. Anne studied hard and did not want Gilbert Blythe to beat her. Gilbert was good-natured about the rivalry, but Anne held grudges and felt strongly about people she hated as well as those she loved. She would not admit she wanted to beat him. Honours went back and forth between them.

paragraphs.context: It was a January the Premier came
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Premier comes to Charlottetown and many Avonlea people go to hear him, leaving Anne and Matthew at home.
paragraphs.simple: A political meeting was held in Charlottetown when the Premier came. Most Avonlea people were on his side and went to town. Mrs. Rachel Lynde, who was on the other side, went too, with her husband and Marilla. Marilla wanted to see a real Premier. Anne and Matthew stayed to keep the house for a day.

paragraphs.context: The program that night was a series of “thrills”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne enjoys every item of the concert, even the old, tired pieces.
paragraphs.simple: For Anne every part of the concert was a thrill. She shivered with pleasure when Prissy Andrews recited, gazed at the ceiling when the choir sang, and laughed at a tired comic piece until others laughed too. When Mr. Phillips gave a famous speech from a play, looking at Prissy at the end of every line, Anne felt that she could rise up against him.

paragraphs.context: “I’m so sorry for people who live in lands
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne talks about Mayflowers and her day out.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says it is sad for people who do not know Mayflowers. She thinks it is tragic not to know them and not to miss them. She thinks Mayflowers are the souls of last summer's flowers. They had lunch by a mossy well and it is fashionable at school to dare each other. Mr. Phillips gave all his flowers to Prissy Andrews.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t think I was crying because I was really so very fond
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne explains why she cried at the teacher's farewell.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she did not cry because she liked Mr. Phillips. She cried because others did. Ruby Gillis began it, although she said she hated him. Anne tried to remember his bad behaviour, but could not stop. Jane Andrews, who said she would not cry, had to borrow a handkerchief.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, Marilla, I’ve had a most fascinating time
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about her tea with the minister's wife and her ideas of goodness.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she has had a wonderful time at tea. Mrs. Allan wore a pretty pink dress and looked like an angel. Anne thinks she would like to be a minister's wife, because a minister would not mind her red hair. But she thinks one must be naturally good, and she is not. She asks if trying hard should count for something.

paragraphs.context: “Everybody has been so good and kind, Marilla,” sighed Anne
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne is recovering from an injury and finds that she has many friends.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she is thankful for how kind everyone has been while she was ill. It shows how many friends she has. Even Superintendent Bell visited, and she is sorry she criticised his prayers. She cannot imagine him as a boy, only with grey whiskers and glasses.

paragraphs.context: “Well, when you can combine patriotism and fun
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about the school concert and her parts in it.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says it is fine to join love of country with fun. There will be choruses, dialogues, recitations and a tableau. She will be Hope, with hands clasped and eyes lifted. She will practise a groan in the garret. Josie Pye is sulky because she did not get the part of fairy queen.

paragraphs.context: MATTHEW was having a bad ten minutes of it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Matthew hides in the kitchen, watches Anne with her friends and sees she is different.
paragraphs.simple: Matthew sat in the woodbox corner to take off his boots, not knowing that Anne and her friends were in the sitting room. They came into the kitchen and he hid shyly. He saw that Anne was different from the others: brighter face, bigger eyes, finer features. This worried him, since it seemed wrong.

paragraphs.context: “They grew in beauty side by side until they were sixteen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells the story she writes for the Story Club, and how she found a proposal hard to imagine.
paragraphs.simple: Anne tells her story about two girls who grew up together, and a man who saved Geraldine's life. She found it hard to imagine a proposal. Ruby told her what she heard when a man proposed to her sister, which Anne thought not romantic. So she imagined it herself.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll settle Miss Anne when she comes home,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marilla is angry that Anne is late and thinks she is full of nonsense.
paragraphs.simple: Marilla speaks angrily and cuts kindling hard. She thinks Anne is out with Diana, writing stories or practising, and not thinking about her duties. She says Anne must be stopped on this. But she has said the same thing she was angry with Rachel Lynde for saying.

paragraphs.context: “I was horribly frightened,” she told Mrs. Allan
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells how she was rescued from the boat under the bridge.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she was very scared as the boat filled with water and drifted. She prayed, but kept her eyes open, because she had to climb onto the bridge posts. She asked God to bring the boat close and said she would do the rest. The boat hit a post and Anne climbed up. She says one does not make a flowery prayer in such a case.

paragraphs.context: “It was splendid,” Anne related to Marilla later on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about the Exhibition and who won prizes.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says the Exhibition was splendid and she liked the horses, flowers and fancywork best. Josie Pye won for knitted lace and Anne was glad she was glad, which shows she is improving. The Sunday-school superintendent won a prize for a pig, which Diana found funny.

paragraphs.context: “Was she? Oh, I’m so sorry I wasn’t in.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells about the Haunted Wood and Diana's mother.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she was in the Haunted Wood with Diana, where the plants sleep for winter. She thinks a grey fairy tucked them under leaves. Diana's mother scolded her for imagining ghosts, which Anne thinks blighted her imagination. Mrs. Lynde says another girl is blighted, which Ruby explains by a boyfriend.

paragraphs.context: “I feel just like studying with might and main,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne is happy to study after the summer and talks about the minister.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she wants to study with all her strength and is glad to see her books again, even geometry. She says the minister preaches fine sermons and Mrs. Lynde fears a city church will take him. She says it is better to enjoy him now. She says if she were a man she would be a minister.

paragraphs.context: “You did just splendidly, Anne,” puffed Diana
paragraphs.mainIdea: Diana runs with the news that Anne has passed the exam in first place.
paragraphs.simple: Diana arrives out of breath with the newspaper. Anne is silent with joy. Diana says all passed, and Anne is at the top. Josie just passed and will be proud anyway. Diana asks how it feels to see her name at the head of the pass list.

paragraphs.context: But suddenly, as her dilated, frightened eyes gazed out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne sees Gilbert in the audience and finds courage to recite.
paragraphs.simple: Anne, afraid, saw Gilbert Blythe at the back with a smile that looked proud and mean to her. In fact he was only enjoying the show. Josie Pye sat next to him and her face was really proud and mean. Anne took a breath, lifted her head and felt courage run through her. She would not fail in front of Gilbert.

paragraphs.context: Anne and the rest of the Avonlea scholars reached town
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne begins school at the Academy and chooses harder work.
paragraphs.simple: The students from Avonlea reached town in time for the Academy. The first day was exciting. Anne planned to do the Second Year work, as Miss Stacy advised, and Gilbert chose the same. This meant a teacher's licence in one year but much more work. The others did the easier course. Anne felt lonely among fifty students, knowing only Gilbert.

paragraphs.context: There was no silly sentiment in Anne’s ideas concerning Gilbert
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne thinks of boys as friends, and thinks Gilbert could be a good one.
paragraphs.simple: Anne had no silly feelings about Gilbert. She thought of boys as possible comrades. She had many girl friends, and thought that boy friendship might be good as well. She imagined walking from the train with Gilbert and talking about their hopes.

paragraphs.context: ON the morning when the final results
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne waits for the exam results with Jane, who is not worried.
paragraphs.simple: On the morning of the results Anne and Jane walked down the street. Jane was happy and sure she had passed, and did not worry because she had no great ambitions. The text says everything has a price, and ambition costs work and worry. Anne was pale and quiet, as in ten minutes she would know who won the medal.

paragraphs.context: Two days afterwards they carried Matthew Cuthbert
paragraphs.mainIdea: After Matthew's death life continues, and Anne feels guilty for feeling joy.
paragraphs.simple: Two days later Matthew was carried away from his home and fields. Avonlea returned to normal and Green Gables slipped into its old habits, with a feeling of loss. Anne, new to grief, thought it sad that things could go on. She felt shame and guilt when she still felt gladness at the sunrise and enjoyed Diana's visits.

paragraphs.context: “Just what I say. I’m not going to take the scholarship.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Anne tells Marilla that she will not go to college but will teach and stay at home.
paragraphs.simple: Anne says she has decided not to take the scholarship, because she cannot leave Marilla alone. Mr. Barry will rent the farm. Anne will teach, at the Carmody school if she cannot get the Avonlea one, living at home and driving there. In winter she can come home on Fridays.

sentences.context: I don’t believe a rose would be as nice if it was called a thistle or a skunk cabbage
sentences.simple: I do not think a rose would be as lovely if it had an ugly name.
sentences.grammar: Anne is saying that a name matters. "Would be ... if it was called" is a pattern for imaginary things. A thistle is a prickly weed and skunk cabbage is a smelly plant, so both have ugly names.

sentences.context: you’ll do that ‘talking to’ you mention with a fair-sized birch switch
sentences.simple: you should punish the child with a stick, not only with words
sentences.grammar: "Talking to" means a telling-off. Mrs. Rachel says the best "language" is to hit the child with a thin stick from a birch tree. In the story's time, many people believed in this kind of punishment.

sentences.context: there’s no scope for imagination in patchwork
sentences.simple: patchwork does not give any space for imagination
sentences.grammar: "Scope" means "room or chance to do something". Anne says that sewing small pieces of cloth together is the same each time, so it is boring for a person who likes to imagine things.

sentences.context: It would be so much easier to imagine I was the Lady Cordelia if I had a real amethyst brooch on
sentences.simple: If I wore a real amethyst brooch it would be easier to pretend to be Lady Cordelia.
sentences.grammar: "It would be ... if I had" is a pattern for unreal things. Anne gives a reason for her act: it would make her game better.

sentences.context: but it is much to be feared that the same thing cannot be said of Anne
sentences.simple: but, sadly, we cannot say the same about Anne
sentences.grammar: The writer talks in an old, formal way. "The same thing cannot be said of Anne" means "Anne was not good-natured about it".

sentences.context: For we pay a price for everything we get or take in this world
sentences.simple: Everything that we get in this world costs us something.
sentences.grammar: The sentence is a wise saying. The writer continues that ambitions need work and sacrifice. "Take" means "accept".

sentences.context: I don’t expect to get it for I understand the trustees have promised it to Gilbert Blythe
sentences.simple: I do not think I will get it, because I hear the school officials have promised it to Gilbert.
sentences.grammar: "Expect to" means "think it will happen". "Trustees" are the people who manage a school. "For" here is an old way to say "because".

depths of despair.example: I’m in the depths of despair

bring up.example: She brought me up by hand

laid up.meaning: Ill in bed and unable to move about.
laid up.example: It isn’t very pleasant to be laid up

all the more.example: it’s all the more to look forward to

look forward to.meaning: To wait for something with pleasure.

right away.example: we can settle the matter right away

heart and soul.example: into her studies heart and soul

pulled up short.meaning: Stopped suddenly and made to change behaviour.

put on airs.meaning: To act as if you are better than others.
put on airs.example: put on as many airs as if she’d led
